blogs.title: Refreshing 7(A): How the D.C. Circuit Handles Stale FOIA Declarations
blogs.description: The panel affirms Exemption 7(A) but spotlights a practical problem in long-running FOIA litigation: staleness. After years passed, the district court required the FBI to update its declarations to confirm that enforcement proceedings were still pending or reasonably anticipated. On appeal, the court accepts a terse follow-on declaration (Bender) because it operated as a time-stamp on earlier, more detailed public and ex parte submissions (Hardy), not as a standalone justification. The post unpacks how this approach reconciles CREW’s warning against vague “ongoing investigation” assertions with deference to law enforcement in national-security matters, and extracts lessons for agencies (periodic updates tied to earlier specifics) and requesters (press for updates; situate ‘passage of time’ arguments within the record’s original level of detail).

blogs.title: Behind Closed Doors: Ex Parte Declarations, Waiver, and FOIA’s National-Security Exception in Practice
blogs.description: Farahi underscores the D.C. Circuit’s continued tolerance of ex parte submissions in national-security FOIA disputes. The district court relied on sealed declarations to assess both interference under 7(A) and segregability; the panel endorses that path, noting the plaintiff did not oppose ex parte treatment and citing Perioperative Services for the proposition that such procedures may be necessary when public reasoning would reveal the very secrets at issue. This post analyzes the doctrinal footing for ex parte review, the role of waiver, and the adversarial deficits it creates. It offers practical strategies for requesters (timely object to ex parte practice, propose alternatives like in camera review of samples or protective summaries) and for agencies (build robust public justifications where feasible while preserving specifics for sealed submissions).

blogs.title: No Meaningful Snippets: Segregability’s Limits When Sensitive Data Is Interspersed
blogs.description: Despite 10,750 pages and 80 CDs of responsive materials, the court affirms that no reasonably segregable, meaningful information could be released. Leaning on Mead Data and Perioperative Services, the opinion emphasizes that FOIA protects ‘information,’ not isolated words, and that line-by-line redaction can be unreasonable when non-exempt material is randomly interspersed and context-laden. This post parses the court’s acceptance of categorical, record-level withholdings in a counterterrorism investigation, the sufficiency of agency affidavits on segregability (including ex parte supplementation), and what this means for Vaughn submissions. It also outlines targeted requester responses, from seeking sample-based in camera review to demanding clearer explanations of why particular document types cannot yield discrete, non-harmful disclosures.

blogs.title: What Counts as ‘Enforcement Proceedings’ Under 7(A)? Elasticity and Deference in Counterterrorism Files
blogs.description: The decision illustrates the D.C. Circuit’s elastic, but not toothless, conception of ‘enforcement proceedings’ in 7(A): ongoing criminal investigations qualify, and the government may establish them by attesting to their existence—especially when bolstered by detailed ex parte showings and broader public context. Anchored in CNSS and Juarez, the court leans on national-security deference and Farahi’s immigration-record allegations to find a continuing, concrete prospective proceeding. This post evaluates the tension with CREW’s demand for more than vague invocations, the risk of de facto indefinite withholding in sprawling counterterrorism investigations, and how courts use public, parallel proceedings to corroborate claims of ongoing law-enforcement activity. It closes with compliance pointers for agencies (tie assertions to identifiable investigative objectives) and for requesters (press for specificity and temporal limiting principles).
